sessions.title: Counting, Representation & Cardinality – Numbers up to 1000
indicators: Read, write and count numbers up to 1000 in numerals and words
Identify place values of 3‑digit numbers (hundreds, tens, ones)
Compare and order numbers using >, <, =
Collaborate with peers to create number charts and games (collaboration)
Use digital counting tools and online games to practise place value (digital literacy)
Think critically to solve number puzzles and explain reasoning (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
Welcome to Numbers up to 1000!

In Basic 2 you learned numbers up to 200. This year we are going all the way to 1000. By the end of this session you will be able to read, write, count, compare and order any number up to 1000.

1. Counting to 1000

Let us count aloud together. Start from 1 and count forward. When we reach 100, we do not stop. We keep going: 101, 102, 103… all the way to 1000.

Counting by ones: 1, 2, 3, …, 99, 100, 101, 102, …, 199, 200, 201, …, 998, 999, 1000.

Counting by tens: 10, 20, 30, …, 100, 110, 120, …, 990, 1000. This helps you reach big numbers quickly.

Counting by hundreds: 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900, 1000.

Activity 1 – Count with the class
Stand in a circle. The teacher points to a pupil who says “1”. The next pupil says “2”, and so on. Try to reach 1000 without making a mistake! When you reach a hundred, everyone claps.

2. Reading and Writing Numerals and Number Words

A numeral is a symbol we write (like 357). A number word tells us how to say it (three hundred and fifty-seven).

Below is a list of important number words you must know.

NumberWord
100One hundred
200Two hundred
300Three hundred
400Four hundred
500Five hundred
600Six hundred
700Seven hundred
800Eight hundred
900Nine hundred
1000One thousand

For numbers in between, we combine the hundred with the tens and ones.

Example 1:
Numeral: 247
Word: Two hundred and forty-seven

Example 2:
Numeral: 605
Word: Six hundred and five

Example 3:
Word: Nine hundred and thirty-two
Numeral: 932

Activity 2 – Flashcard match
Make 20 cards. On ten cards write numerals (e.g., 384, 720). On the other ten write the matching words. Shuffle the cards and work with a partner to match them. Time yourselves – can you beat your last time?

3. Place Value – Hundreds, Tens, Ones

Every digit in a number has a place value. For 3‑digit numbers the places are Hundreds (H), Tens (T), Ones (O).

Look at the number 462.

  • The digit 4 is in the hundreds place → 4 hundreds = 400
  • The digit 6 is in the tens place → 6 tens = 60
  • The digit 2 is in the ones place → 2 ones = 2

So 462 = 400 + 60 + 2.

We can draw a place value chart:

HundredsTensOnes
462

Zero holds a place. If there are no tens, we write 0.

Example: 508 = 5 hundreds + 0 tens + 8 ones.

HTO
508

Activity 3 – Build with base‑ten materials
If you have base‑ten blocks, use hundreds flats, tens rods and ones cubes. The teacher calls a number like 734. You build it: 7 flats, 3 rods, 4 cubes. If you do not have blocks, draw squares for hundreds, lines for tens and dots for ones.

Digital corner: Visit an online place‑value chart (your teacher will show you). Drag digits into the hundreds, tens and ones columns to form numbers. Watch how the total changes.

4. Comparing Numbers – Greater Than, Less Than, Equal To

We use symbols to compare numbers:

  • > means “is greater than”
  • < means “is less than”
  • = means “is equal to”

Always start by comparing the hundreds digit. If they are the same, compare the tens. If those are also the same, compare the ones.

Example 1: Compare 573 and 489.
Hundreds: 5 hundreds (500) vs 4 hundreds (400). Since 500 > 400, we write: 573 > 489.

Example 2: Compare 628 and 635.
Hundreds are both 600 → equal. Look at tens: 2 tens (20) vs 3 tens (30). Since 20 < 30, we write: 628 < 635.

Example 3: Compare 801 and 801.
All digits match, so they are equal: 801 = 801.

Activity 4 – Number duel
Work in pairs. Each pupil writes a 3‑digit number secretly. Reveal your numbers at the same time. Together decide which symbol (>, < or =) goes between them. Write the comparison in your exercise book. Do this ten times. Switch partners.

5. Ordering Numbers

Ordering means writing numbers from smallest to largest (ascending) or largest to smallest (descending).

Example: Order these numbers from smallest to largest: 312, 309, 325, 299.
First compare hundreds: all have 3 hundreds except 299 (2 hundreds). So 299 is the smallest.
Now among 309, 312, 325 – compare tens: 0, 1, 2 → order: 309, 312, 325.
So the ascending order is: 299, 309, 312, 325.
Descending order is the reverse: 325, 312, 309, 299.

Activity 5 – Human number line
Ten pupils each hold a card with a different 3‑digit number. Without talking, arrange yourselves in a line from smallest to largest. The rest of the class checks. How fast can you do it?

Puzzle corner (critical thinking):
I am thinking of a number. It is greater than 650 but less than 700. Its tens digit is 8. The sum of its digits is 20. What is my number? (Answer: 686)

Activity 6 – Design a number chart (collaboration)
In groups of four, create a colourful poster of numbers from 1 to 1000. Use a 10×10 grid for each hundred. Mark counting patterns (e.g., all numbers with 5 in the ones place in red). Present your chart to the class and explain the pattern.

Exercise 1.1

Answer the following in your exercise book.

  1. Write in words:
    (a) 482
    (b) 710
    (c) 999
  2. Write in numerals:
    (a) Five hundred and sixty-one
    (b) Three hundred and eight
    (c) One thousand
  3. Complete the place value table for 758.
  4. Fill in with >, < or = :
    (a) 435 ____ 453
    (b) 800 ____ 800
    (c) 679 ____ 697
  5. Order these numbers from smallest to largest: 901, 109, 190, 910.
  6. The number is 5 hundreds + 1 ten + 7 ones. What is it?
  7. Write the number that is 10 more than 690.

Challenge: Use three different digits to make the largest possible 3‑digit number and the smallest possible 3‑digit number. Write the two numbers and compare them.

sessions.title: Skip Counting and Number Patterns
indicators: Skip count forwards and backwards in 2s, 3s, 5s, 10s, 50s, 100s up to 1000
Complete and extend number patterns
Work in groups to create and share skip‑counting songs or rhythms (collaboration, creativity)
Use spreadsheet or interactive whiteboard to generate skip‑counting sequences (digital literacy)
Persist through challenging patterns to develop personal resilience (personal development)
sessions.content:
Skip Counting – Let's Jump Ahead!

Skip counting is like hopping over some numbers and landing on others. You do not say every number; you skip a fixed number of steps each time.

1. Skip Counting Forwards

Counting by 2s: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, …, 98, 100, 102, …, 998, 1000. Notice all these numbers are even.

Counting by 3s: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, …, 99, 102, …, 999. Try to say them quickly!

Counting by 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20, …, 95, 100, 105, …, 995, 1000. Numbers end in 0 or 5.

Counting by 10s: 10, 20, 30, …, 100, 110, …, 1000. Easiest! Just add a zero.

Counting by 50s: 50, 100, 150, 200, …, 950, 1000.

Counting by 100s: 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900, 1000.

2. Skip Counting Backwards

You can also skip count backwards – this is like counting down.

Example: Count backwards by 10s from 1000: 1000, 990, 980, 970, …, 100, 90, …, 10.

Example: Backwards by 5s from 100: 100, 95, 90, 85, …, 5, 0.

Activity 1 – Number ball toss
Stand in a circle. The teacher starts with 0 and tosses a ball to a pupil who says the next number in the skip‑counting sequence (e.g., by 3s). That pupil tosses to another, who says the next, and so on. If you say the wrong number, sit down. How long can the chain last?

3. Number Patterns

A number pattern is a sequence where numbers change in a regular way. To continue a pattern, find the rule.

Example 1: 5, 10, 15, 20, ___, ___, ___
Rule: Add 5 each time. Next numbers: 25, 30, 35.

Example 2: 100, 90, 80, 70, ___, ___, ___
Rule: Subtract 10 each time. Next numbers: 60, 50, 40.

Example 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, ___, ___, ___
Rule: Add 3. Next numbers: 15, 18, 21.

Example 4: 1, 4, 7, 10, ___, ___
Rule: Add 3. Next numbers: 13, 16.

Activity 2 – Pattern detectives
In pairs, one pupil writes a pattern (at least 5 numbers) and leaves three blanks. The partner must find the rule and fill in the blanks. Swap roles.

Activity 3 – Create a skip‑counting song or rhyme
In groups of four, make up a fun song, chant or rhythm that helps you remember skip counting by a certain number (e.g., a clapping game for the 3 times table). Perform it for the class. (creativity, collaboration)

Digital corner: Open a spreadsheet program (like Excel or Google Sheets). Type 0 in cell A1, then =A1+3 in cell A2. Drag the formula down to see the sequence generated automatically. Try different skip steps (digital literacy).

Exercise 1.2

  1. Continue each sequence by writing the next three numbers:
    (a) 50, 100, 150, 200, ___, ___, ___
    (b) 990, 980, 970, 960, ___, ___, ___
    (c) 6, 12, 18, 24, ___, ___, ___
  2. Write the skip‑counting pattern for 4s from 4 to 40.
  3. What is the rule for this pattern? 110, 120, 130, 140, …
  4. Create your own pattern. Write the first six numbers and then explain the rule.
  5. Count backwards by 50s from 1000 to 0. Write the sequence.

sessions.title: Addition and Subtraction within 1000
indicators: Add two 3‑digit numbers without and with regrouping
Subtract two 3‑digit numbers with borrowing
Solve real‑life word problems involving addition and subtraction
Work collaboratively to solve multi‑step word problems and explain strategies (collaboration, communication)
Use digital simulations or apps to model regrouping (digital literacy)
Reflect on different problem‑solving methods and justify choices (critical thinking, personal development)
sessions.content:
Addition and Subtraction – Working with Big Numbers

Now we will add and subtract numbers up to 1000. We must be careful with regrouping (carrying and borrowing).

1. Addition without Regrouping

Add the ones, then tens, then hundreds.

Example: 324 + 152
Ones: 4 + 2 = 6
Tens: 2 + 5 = 7
Hundreds: 3 + 1 = 4
Answer: 476

2. Addition with Regrouping (Carrying)

When the sum in a column is 10 or more, we regroup.

Example: 378 + 255
Ones: 8 + 5 = 13 → write 3, carry 1 to tens.
Tens: 7 + 5 + 1 = 13 → write 3, carry 1 to hundreds.
Hundreds: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6
Answer: 633

Activity 1 – Roll and Add
Use three dice. Roll to create two 3‑digit numbers (e.g., first roll: 4,2,6 → 426; second roll: 3,5,1 → 351). Add them. Do ten sums. Check with a partner.

3. Subtraction without Borrowing

Subtract ones, then tens, then hundreds. Make sure the top number is larger.

Example: 685 – 342
Ones: 5 – 2 = 3
Tens: 8 – 4 = 4
Hundreds: 6 – 3 = 3
Answer: 343

4. Subtraction with Borrowing (Regrouping)

If a digit on top is smaller than the one below, we borrow from the next higher place.

Example: 542 – 278
Ones: 2 – 8? Cannot. Borrow 1 ten from 4 tens → 12 – 8 = 4. Now tens: 3 tens – 7 tens? Cannot. Borrow 1 hundred from 5 hundreds → 13 tens – 7 tens = 6 tens. Hundreds: 4 – 2 = 2. Answer: 264.

Activity 2 – Base‑ten block subtraction
Use base‑ten blocks to model borrowing. Show 542 as 5 flats, 4 rods, 2 cubes. Try to remove 278 by exchanging a flat for 10 rods, etc. (Use digital base‑ten apps if available – digital literacy).

5. Word Problems

Example 1: Ama had 456 stickers. She bought 238 more. How many stickers does she have now?
456 + 238 = 694 stickers.

Example 2: A school has 800 pupils. 435 are boys. How many are girls?
800 – 435 = 365 girls.

Activity 3 – Write your own problem
Work in pairs. Each pair writes a word problem using 3‑digit numbers. Swap with another pair and solve. Discuss the answers. (collaboration, communication)

Critical thinking: Can you solve 804 – 357 in two different ways? (e.g., borrow across zeros, or break numbers apart). Discuss which method you find easier and why.

Exercise 1.3

  1. Add:
    (a) 432 + 245
    (b) 567 + 189
    (c) 704 + 238
  2. Subtract:
    (a) 876 – 543
    (b) 700 – 382
    (c) 903 – 617
  3. A farmer had 530 oranges. He sold 287. How many are left?
  4. Kofi read 215 pages on Monday and 178 on Tuesday. How many pages did he read altogether?
  5. The sum of two numbers is 900. One number is 456. What is the other?

sessions.title: Multiplication and Division
indicators: Multiply 2‑digit by 1‑digit numbers using arrays, repeated addition and area models
Recall multiplication facts for 1–5 and 10
Divide 2‑digit numbers by 1‑digit numbers (with and without remainders)
Solve real‑life problems involving multiplication and division
Design visual posters or arrays to explain multiplication facts (creativity)
Use digital quizzes to practise times tables and receive instant feedback (digital literacy)
Work in pairs to peer‑assess multiplication/division solutions (collaboration, communication)
sessions.content:
Multiplication – Repeated Addition Made Easy

Multiplication is a quick way of adding the same number many times. For example, 5 + 5 + 5 = 3 × 5 = 15.

1. Multiplication as Repeated Addition

If you have 4 bags with 6 oranges in each, you have 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24 oranges. That is 4 × 6 = 24.

Example: 3 × 7 = 7 + 7 + 7 = 21

2. Using Arrays

An array is an arrangement of objects in rows and columns. 4 rows of 5 stars gives 4 × 5 = 20.

Draw dots or counters to show arrays for the 2, 3, 4, 5 and 10 times tables.

Activity 1 – Array city
On squared paper, draw arrays for multiplication facts up to 10×10. Colour them and label each with the multiplication sentence. Display them as a class ‘Array City’. (creativity)

3. Multiplication Tables to Memorise

  • 1 times table: any number × 1 = itself
  • 2 times table: doubling
  • 3 times table: triple
  • 4 times table: double twice
  • 5 times table: skip count by 5
  • 10 times table: just add a zero

Activity 2 – Times table rap
Create a rap or song for the 3 times table. Perform it for the class. (creativity, collaboration)

4. Multiplying 2‑Digit by 1‑Digit

Break the 2‑digit number into tens and ones.

Example: 23 × 3
20 × 3 = 60
3 × 3 = 9
60 + 9 = 69

Or use the standard algorithm:

  23
× 3
――
  69  (3×3=9; 3×20=60)

Example: 45 × 6
40 × 6 = 240; 5 × 6 = 30; total 270

Activity 3 – Roll and multiply
Roll a die to get a 1‑digit number. Roll two dice to make a 2‑digit number. Multiply them. Do 15 problems. Check with a partner. (collaboration)

5. Division – Sharing Equally

Division is splitting a number into equal parts.

Example: 24 ÷ 4 = ? means “How many groups of 4 in 24?” Answer: 6.

You can think: 4 × __ = 24 → 6.

Division with remainders: 29 ÷ 3 = ? 3 × 9 = 27, remainder 2. So 29 ÷ 3 = 9 r 2.

Activity 4 – Fair shares
Use counters. Count out 37 counters. Share them equally among 5 friends. How many each? How many left? (Answer: 7 each, 2 left).

Digital corner: Use an online multiplication/division quiz game (e.g., Kahoot, Mathplayground) to practise times tables and get instant feedback. (digital literacy)

Exercise 1.4

  1. Write as multiplication: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = ____ × ____
  2. Multiply:
    (a) 7 × 4
    (b) 9 × 5
    (c) 6 × 10
  3. Draw an array for 5 × 3.
  4. Multiply:
    (a) 32 × 4
    (b) 51 × 7
    (c) 43 × 8
  5. Divide:
    (a) 36 ÷ 6
    (b) 45 ÷ 9
    (c) 28 ÷ 5 (write the remainder)
  6. A teacher has 80 crayons. She gives 5 crayons to each pupil. How many pupils get crayons?
  7. There are 4 shelves. Each shelf holds 23 books. How many books in total?

sessions.title: Fractions
indicators: Recognise ½, ¼, ⅓, ⅕, ¹⁄₁₀ as equal parts of a whole or a set
Compare fractions with the same denominator using visual models
Add and subtract fractions with like denominators
Use manipulatives (fraction circles, paper folding) creatively to represent fractions (creativity)
Explain fraction comparisons to a partner using appropriate language (communication)
Connect fractions to everyday sharing situations (cultural identity, global citizenship – fair sharing)
sessions.content:
Fractions – Parts of a Whole

A fraction tells us what part of a whole or a group we are talking about. The bottom number (denominator) tells how many equal parts the whole is divided into. The top number (numerator) tells how many parts we have.

1. Unit Fractions

½ (one‑half) – one part out of two equal parts.
¼ (one‑quarter) – one part out of four equal parts.
⅓ (one‑third) – one part out of three equal parts.
⅕ (one‑fifth) – one part out of five equal parts.
¹⁄₁₀ (one‑tenth) – one part out of ten equal parts.

Activity 1 – Paper folding
Take a square paper. Fold it into two equal parts and shade ½. Then fold another into four equal parts and shade ¼. Compare the sizes. Which is bigger? (communication – explain to partner).

2. Comparing Fractions with Like Denominators

When denominators are the same, compare the numerators.

Example: ²⁄₄ and ¾ → 2 < 3 so ²⁄₄ < ¾

Draw fraction strips or use fraction circles to see this.

Activity 2 – Fraction war
Each player has a set of fraction cards with the same denominator (e.g., fourths: ¼, ²⁄₄, ¾, ⁴⁄₄). Shuffle, each flips one card, the larger fraction wins. (creativity – make your own cards).

3. Adding and Subtracting Fractions with Like Denominators

Only add or subtract the numerators. Keep the same denominator.

Example: ⅕ + ²⁄₅ = ³⁄₅
Example: ⁶⁄₈ – ²⁄₈ = ⁴⁄₈ (which simplifies to ½, but in Basic 3 we leave it as ⁴⁄₈ or simplify if taught).

Activity 3 – Fraction pizza
Draw a circle (pizza). Divide it into 8 equal slices. Shade ³⁄₈ with one colour and ²⁄₈ with another. How many slices are shaded in total? What fraction? (³⁄₈ + ²⁄₈ = ⁵⁄₈).

Life connection: When sharing food (like banku or bread) with family, discuss how to divide it into equal parts so everyone gets a fair share. (cultural identity, citizenship)

Exercise 1.5

  1. What fraction of each shape is shaded? (Draw or describe).
  2. Write the fraction for: one part out of five equal parts.
  3. Compare using > or <: (a) ½ ___ ¼ (Hint: draw) (b) ³⁄₅ ___ ²⁄₅.
  4. Add: (a) ⅓ + ⅓ = (b) ²⁄₇ + ³⁄₇ =
  5. Subtract: (a) ⁵⁄₆ – ¹⁄₆ = (b) ⁴⁄₅ – ²⁄₅ =
  6. Kofi ate ⅛ of a cake. Ama ate ³⁄₈. What fraction did they eat together?

sessions.title: Money
indicators: Count Ghana cedis and pesewas up to GH₵ 100
Make change in simple buying and selling transactions
Solve real‑life problems involving money
Role‑play market scenes to practise transactions and develop communication skills (communication, cultural identity)
Discuss the value of saving and wise spending (personal development, citizenship)
Use digital money‑simulation apps to practise making change (digital literacy)
sessions.content:
Money – Ghana Cedis and Pesewas

In Ghana, we use cedis (GH₵) and pesewas (Gp). 100 pesewas = 1 cedi.

1. Recognising Coins and Notes

Coins: 1Gp, 5Gp, 10Gp, 20Gp, 50Gp, GH₵1
Notes: GH₵1, GH₵2, GH₵5, GH₵10, GH₵20, GH₵50, GH₵100

Activity 1 – Coin rubbings
Place paper over real coins and rub with a pencil. Label each coin with its value. Create a poster. (creativity)

2. Counting Money

Always start with the largest value and add the smaller ones.

Example: You have GH₵20, GH₵10, GH₵5, GH₵2, 50Gp, 20Gp, 10Gp.
Total: 20 + 10 + 5 + 2 = 37 cedis. Pesewas: 50 + 20 + 10 = 80Gp. So GH₵37.80.

Activity 2 – Shopkeeper simulation (role‑play)
Set up a mini shop with items priced between 50Gp and GH₵50. Customers pay with notes and coins; shopkeeper counts out change. Rotate roles. (communication, cultural identity – familiar marketplace language).

3. Making Change

To find change: subtract the cost from the amount paid.

Example: You buy a book for GH₵12.50 and pay with GH₵20.00.
Change = 20.00 – 12.50 = GH₵7.50.

Activity 3 – Change challenge
Teacher calls out a price and an amount paid. Pupils quickly write the change. First correct answer wins a point.

4. Saving and Spending Wisely

Discuss: Why is it good to save some of your money? How can you plan what to buy with your money? (personal development, citizenship).

Digital corner: Use a virtual money app (like “My Money” or an online cash register simulation) to practise transactions and make change. (digital literacy)

Exercise 1.6

  1. Write the total:
    (a) GH₵50 + GH₵20 + GH₵5 =
    (b) 50Gp + 20Gp + 10Gp + 10Gp =
  2. Kofi bought a pencil for GH₵2.50 and an eraser for GH₵1.00. He gave the shopkeeper GH₵10. How much change did he get?
  3. You have GH₵15.00. You want to buy a book (GH₵9.50) and a pen (GH₵3.00). Can you afford both? Explain.
  4. Ama saved GH₵12.00 in January and GH₵18.50 in February. How much did she save altogether?
  5. Draw the coins and notes you would use to pay GH₵27.30 exactly.

sessions.title: Patterns and Relationships
indicators: Describe, extend and create repeating and growing patterns using shapes, objects and numbers
Find missing elements in a pattern
Work in groups to design and present original patterns (creativity, collaboration)
Use digital drawing tools to create and extend patterns (digital literacy)
Think critically to predict the next elements and justify predictions (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
Patterns – What Comes Next?

A pattern is something that repeats or grows in a predictable way. Patterns can be made of shapes, colours, objects, or numbers.

1. Repeating Patterns

A repeating pattern has a core unit that repeats again and again.

Example: Circle, Triangle, Circle, Triangle, … The core is “Circle, Triangle” and it repeats.

Example: Red, Blue, Blue, Red, Blue, Blue, … Core: “Red, Blue, Blue”.

Activity 1 – Sound patterns
Make a sound pattern with claps and taps. For example: clap, tap, tap, clap, tap, tap, … Can your partner continue the pattern?

2. Growing Patterns

Growing patterns increase or decrease by a rule each step.

Example: 1, 3, 5, 7, … Rule: Start at 1, add 2 each time.

Example with shapes: 1 square, 2 squares, 3 squares (the number of squares grows by 1 each time).

Activity 2 – Pattern station
In groups, rotate between stations that have pattern cards. At each station, find the rule and extend the pattern by at least four more terms. Discuss your answers. (collaboration, critical thinking)

3. Finding Missing Elements

Look for the rule, then fill in the blanks.

Example: 4, __, 12, 16, __, 24. Rule: add 4. Missing: 8 and 20.

Activity 3 – Create your own pattern
Use coloured beads, bottle tops, or drawing software to design a repeating or growing pattern. Show it to the class and ask them to explain the rule. (creativity, digital literacy if using drawing software)

Exercise 2.1

  1. What is the core of this repeating pattern? 🌞🌛🌞🌛🌞🌛
  2. Draw the next three shapes: ♦ ● ● ♦ ● ● ____ ____ ____
  3. Extend the number pattern: 10, 20, 30, __, __, __
  4. Find the missing numbers: 2, 4, __, 8, __, 12 (rule: add 2).
  5. Create a growing pattern of your own using numbers. Write the first five terms and explain the rule.

sessions.title: Equality and Simple Equations
indicators: Complete number sentences (e.g., 7 + ___ = 12)
Write and solve simple equations using symbols or boxes (e.g., □ + 5 = 9)
Explain the meaning of the equal sign as balance (communication, critical thinking)
Create their own ‘mystery number’ problems for peers (creativity)
Use interactive balance‑scale apps to explore equality (digital literacy)
sessions.content:
Equality – Keeping the Balance

The equal sign (=) means “is the same as”. Think of it like a balance scale. Both sides must be equal.

1. Completing Number Sentences

You can find a missing number by using the opposite operation.

Example: 7 + ___ = 12
Think: 12 – 7 = 5, so the missing number is 5.

Example: ___ – 4 = 10
Think: 10 + 4 = 14, so the missing number is 14.

Activity 1 – Balance scale model
Draw a balance scale. On the left side write 8 + □. On the right side write 15. Ask: What number goes in the box to make the scale balance? (□ = 7). (communication – explain your thinking).

2. Equations with Symbols

We can use a box (□) or a letter (n) for the unknown number.

Example: n + 5 = 9 → n = 4
Example: 20 – y = 12 → y = 8

Activity 2 – Mystery number envelopes
Write an equation on an envelope, e.g., “□ + 6 = 11”. Inside, put the answer. Exchange envelopes with a partner and solve. (creativity, collaboration)

Digital corner: Use an online balance‑scale interactive (e.g., NLVM balance) where you drag weights to solve simple equations. (digital literacy)

Exercise 2.2

  1. Find the missing number:
    (a) 9 + ___ = 16
    (b) ___ + 7 = 20
    (c) 18 – ___ = 5
  2. Write the equation and solve: A number plus 8 equals 15. What is the number?
  3. Use a box or letter: □ – 6 = 7. Find □.
  4. Solve for n: 3 × n = 12. Hint: n = 12 ÷ 3.
  5. Create a “mystery number” problem for your classmate to solve. Write it on a card.

sessions.title: 2D and 3D Shapes
indicators: Identify and name 2D shapes: square, rectangle, triangle, circle, pentagon, hexagon
Identify and name 3D objects: cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone
Describe properties of shapes (number of sides, vertices, faces, edges)
Draw and model 2D shapes; build 3D models from nets or clay
Collaboratively sort and classify shapes using different criteria (collaboration, critical thinking)
Use digital geometry tools (e.g., interactive whiteboard shape libraries) to explore shapes (digital literacy)
sessions.content:
Shapes All Around Us

Shapes are everywhere. Some are flat (2D), and some are solid (3D). Let's learn their names and properties.

1. 2D (Flat) Shapes

  • Square: 4 equal sides, 4 corners (vertices).
  • Rectangle: 4 sides, opposite sides equal, 4 corners.
  • Triangle: 3 sides, 3 corners.
  • Circle: no sides, no corners, round.
  • Pentagon: 5 sides, 5 corners.
  • Hexagon: 6 sides, 6 corners.

Activity 1 – Shape hunt
Walk around the classroom and school compound. Find objects that look like each 2D shape. Record them in a table. (collaboration – work in pairs).

2. 3D (Solid) Objects

  • Cube: 6 equal square faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. Example: dice.
  • Cuboid: 6 rectangular faces (may have square faces), 12 edges, 8 vertices. Example: matchbox.
  • Sphere: no faces, no edges, no vertices; perfectly round. Example: ball.
  • Cylinder: 2 circular faces, 1 curved surface. Example: tin of milk.
  • Cone: 1 circular face, 1 curved surface, 1 vertex (apex). Example: party hat.

Activity 2 – Build 3D models
Use clay, toothpicks and bottle caps to build a cube, cuboid, cylinder and cone. Count faces, edges and vertices. (creativity, collaboration).

Activity 3 – Shape sorting
In groups, sort a collection of shapes into two groups using your own rules (e.g., shapes with straight edges vs. curved edges; 2D vs. 3D). Share your rules. (critical thinking).

Digital corner: Use a virtual geoboard or shape‑drawing tool (e.g., Geogebra, interactive whiteboard shape gallery) to create and label shapes. (digital literacy)

Exercise 3.1

  1. Name the shape with 5 sides.
  2. How many vertices does a triangle have?
  3. What 3D object is shaped like a tin of Milo?
  4. Complete: A cube has ___ faces, ___ edges, ___ vertices.
  5. Draw a rectangle and a triangle. Label their sides and vertices.
  6. Give two differences between a square and a rectangle.

sessions.title: Length and Mass
indicators: Estimate and measure length in centimetres (cm) and metres (m)
Compare and order lengths of objects
Estimate and measure mass in grams (g) and kilograms (kg)
Solve real‑life problems involving length and mass
Work in pairs to measure and record classroom objects, discussing accuracy (collaboration, communication)
Use digital scales and measurement apps to collect data (digital literacy)
Reflect on the importance of accurate measurement in daily life (personal development)
sessions.content:
Measuring Length and Mass

We measure length to find out how long or tall something is. We measure mass to find out how heavy something is.

1. Length – Centimetres and Metres

Short lengths are measured in centimetres (cm). 100 cm = 1 metre (m).
A ruler is usually 30 cm long. A metre stick is 100 cm.

Estimating: First guess the length, then measure to check.

Example: About how many centimetres long is your pencil? Estimate: 15 cm. Measure with a ruler: 14 cm. Good estimate!

Activity 1 – Measure your world
In pairs, measure the length of your desk, your maths book, your shoe, and the width of the classroom. Record in a table with columns: Object, Estimate, Actual. (collaboration, communication).

2. Mass – Grams and Kilograms

Gram (g) is a small unit of mass. A paperclip weighs about 1 g.
Kilogram (kg) = 1000 g. A bag of sugar is often 1 kg.

We use a balance or a scale to measure mass.

Activity 2 – Weighing station
Use a simple balance or digital scale (if available). Weigh objects like an eraser, a textbook, a full water bottle. Estimate first, then weigh. Compare your estimates. (digital literacy if using digital scale).

3. Solving Problems

Example: A rope is 250 cm long. Another rope is 175 cm long. What is their total length? 250 + 175 = 425 cm or 4 m 25 cm.

Example: A bag of rice is 5 kg. A bag of beans is 3 kg. What is the difference? 5 – 3 = 2 kg.

Reflection: Why is it important to measure accurately when a tailor sews a dress or a carpenter builds a table? (personal development, real‑life connection).

Exercise 3.2

  1. Which unit would you use to measure the length of a football field: cm or m?
  2. Estimate the length of your arm in cm. Then measure it.
  3. Convert: 3 m = ___ cm.
  4. A bag of cement weighs 50 kg. How many kilograms do 2 bags weigh?
  5. You have 2 kg of flour. You use 500 g to bake bread. How much flour is left? (1 kg = 1000 g).
  6. Order these masses from lightest to heaviest: 800 g, 2 kg, 1500 g, 1 kg.

sessions.title: Capacity
indicators: Estimate and measure capacity in litres (L) and millilitres (mL)
Compare and order the volumes of different containers
Solve problems involving capacity
Design a simple investigation to compare capacities and record results (creativity, critical thinking)
Use digital simulations (virtual measuring jugs) to practise reading scales (digital literacy)
Discuss the importance of careful measurement when cooking or sharing drinks (cultural identity)
sessions.content:
Capacity – How Much Does It Hold?

Capacity is the amount of liquid a container can hold. We measure capacity in litres (L) and millilitres (mL). 1000 mL = 1 L.

1. Litres and Millilitres

A small water bottle holds about 500 mL. A big bottle of soft drink is often 1 L or 1.5 L. A teaspoon holds about 5 mL.

Estimating: Guess the capacity, then fill with water and pour into a measuring jug to check.

Activity 1 – Container collection
Bring empty containers (water bottles, milk tins, Fanta bottles). Estimate their capacities and then measure using a measuring jug. Record your results. Which was closest?

2. Comparing Capacities

Order containers from the one that holds the least to the one that holds the most.

Example: A cup holds 250 mL. A bowl holds 1 L. A bucket holds 10 L. Order: cup (250 mL), bowl (1 L = 1000 mL), bucket (10 L).

Activity 2 – Investigation
Design an experiment to find out how many cups of water fill a 1‑litre bottle. Predict, then test. Record your steps and results. (creativity, critical thinking).

3. Solving Problems

Example: A bottle contains 1 L of juice. You pour 350 mL into a cup. How much juice is left? 1 L = 1000 mL, 1000 – 350 = 650 mL.

Cultural connection: When cooking fufu or banku, measuring the water correctly is important to get the right texture. (cultural identity).

Digital corner: Use an interactive measuring cylinder simulation online to practise reading the scale for different volumes. (digital literacy).

Exercise 3.3

  1. How many millilitres are in 2 litres?
  2. Which holds more: a 500 mL bottle or a 1 L carton?
  3. A jerrycan holds 20 L of water. You use 7 L to wash. How much remains?
  4. Order these capacities from smallest to largest: 2 L, 1500 mL, 750 mL, 3 L.
  5. Estimate the capacity of your school water cup. Then ask your teacher to help you measure it.

sessions.title: Time
indicators: Read and write time on analogue and digital clocks to 5‑minute intervals
Calculate elapsed time in hours and minutes
Use a calendar to identify days, weeks, months and years
Work in groups to create a daily schedule and explain time management (collaboration, personal development)
Use digital clock tools and stopwatches to measure time intervals (digital literacy)
Reflect on punctuality and the value of time in Ghanaian culture (cultural identity)
sessions.content:
Telling Time – Clocks and Calendars

We use time every day to plan our activities. There are two common types of clocks: analogue (with hands) and digital (shows numbers).

1. Reading Analogue Clocks to 5 Minutes

The short hand tells the hour. The long hand tells the minutes. Each number on the clock represents 5 minutes.

Example: If the short hand is just past 7 and the long hand points to 4 (which means 20 minutes), the time is 7:20.

Example: Long hand at 9 → 45 minutes; time is quarter to the next hour.

Activity 1 – Make a clock
Use a paper plate, write numbers, attach hands with a split pin. Practise showing times that the teacher calls out (e.g., “half past 9”, “10:25”).

2. Digital Clocks

Digital clocks show hours and minutes separated by a colon (:). 08:15 is 8:15 AM. 14:30 is 2:30 PM (24‑hour clock may be introduced).

Activity 2 – Time match
Match analogue clock cards to digital time cards. (collaboration).

3. Elapsed Time

To find how much time passes, count forward from the start time to the end time.

Example: School starts at 8:00 and ends at 2:30. From 8:00 to 2:00 is 6 hours, plus 30 minutes → 6 hours 30 minutes.

Activity 3 – Daily schedule poster
In groups, create a timeline of your school day with start and end times. Calculate the length of each activity. (collaboration, personal development).

4. Calendar – Days, Weeks, Months

7 days = 1 week. About 4 weeks = 1 month. 12 months = 1 year.

Example: If today is 5th July, what date will it be in 2 weeks? 5 + 14 = 19th July.

Cultural reflection: Discuss why being on time (punctuality) is valued in Ghanaian society. How does it show respect? (cultural identity, personal development).

Digital corner: Use an online stopwatch to time how long it takes to run 100 metres or complete a maths drill. Record the times. (digital literacy).

Exercise 3.4

  1. Draw an analogue clock showing 4:35.
  2. Write the digital time for half past 9 in the morning.
  3. If a lesson starts at 9:15 and ends at 10:00, how many minutes long is it?
  4. If today is 12th March, what date will it be in 3 weeks?
  5. How many days are there in July and August altogether?
  6. You leave home at 7:20 and arrive at school at 7:50. How long was your journey?

sessions.title: Perimeter and Area (Introduction)
indicators: Measure the perimeter of simple 2D shapes using non‑standard and standard units (cm, m)
Find the area of shapes by counting unit squares
Design a small garden or playground layout and calculate its perimeter and area (creativity, critical thinking)
Work in pairs to measure and compare perimeters of objects around the school (collaboration)
Use digital graphing paper or apps to explore area (digital literacy)
sessions.content:
Perimeter and Area – The Fence and the Field

Perimeter is the distance around the outside of a shape. Think of a fence around a garden.
Area is the amount of space inside the shape. Think of the grass inside the garden.

1. Perimeter

To find the perimeter, add the lengths of all sides.

Example: A rectangle is 5 cm long and 3 cm wide. Its perimeter = 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm. You can also do (2×5) + (2×3) = 10 + 6 = 16 cm.

Activity 1 – Measure the perimeter
Use a ruler to measure the sides of your maths book. Calculate its perimeter. Then measure the perimeter of the classroom floor using metre sticks or steps (non‑standard: paces). Compare results. (collaboration).

2. Area by Counting Squares

To find area, we count how many unit squares fit inside the shape.

Example: Draw a rectangle on 1 cm grid paper that is 4 cm long and 2 cm wide. It contains 8 small squares. The area is 8 square centimetres (8 cm²).

Activity 2 – Grid picture
On centimetre grid paper, draw a shape of your choice (robot, house). Count the squares to find its area. (creativity).

3. Design Project

In pairs, design a simple playground or garden on grid paper. Show the perimeter fence length and the area of grass. (critical thinking, collaboration).

Digital corner: Use an online virtual geoboard or area grid tool (e.g., Area Builder by PhET) to create shapes and see their area and perimeter. (digital literacy).

Exercise 3.5

  1. Find the perimeter of a square with sides of 7 cm.
  2. A rectangle is 8 m by 3 m. What is its perimeter?
  3. Draw a shape on grid paper that has an area of 10 square units. What is its perimeter?
  4. Count the squares to find the area of a 5 cm by 3 cm rectangle drawn on grid paper.
  5. Why do you think a farmer needs to know the perimeter and area of his field?

sessions.title: Data Collection and Representation
indicators: Collect data using tally marks and simple questionnaires
Represent data in pictographs and bar charts (1‑to‑1 and 1‑to‑2 scales)
Interpret and discuss information from graphs
Work collaboratively to design a class survey and present findings (collaboration, communication, creativity)
Use digital spreadsheet or graphing software to create charts (digital literacy)
Critically question misleading or unclear graphs (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
Data – Telling Stories with Numbers

Data is information we collect to learn more about the world. We can show data in graphs to make it easy to understand.

1. Collecting Data with Tally Marks

A tally is a mark that helps you count. Each time you count one, draw a line. When you get to 5, draw a diagonal line through the first four.

Example: Favourite fruits: Mango – |||| (4), Orange – 卌 (5), Banana – ||| (3).

Activity 1 – Class survey
In groups, choose a question (e.g., “What is your favourite colour?”). Ask every pupil in the class and record their answers using a tally chart. (collaboration, communication).

2. Pictographs

A pictograph uses pictures or symbols to represent data. Each picture might stand for 1 person (or 2 if using a 1‑to‑2 scale).

Example: Favourite pet: 🐶🐶🐶🐶 (4 dogs), 🐱🐱🐱 (3 cats).

Activity 2 – Draw a pictograph
Use your survey results to create a pictograph on chart paper. Remember to include a key (e.g., 1 smiley = 2 pupils). (creativity).

3. Bar Charts

A bar chart uses bars of different heights to show data. The height of the bar tells the number.

Example: If 10 pupils like football and 6 like netball, the football bar is taller. Label axes: “Sport” and “Number of pupils”.

Activity 3 – Bar chart on squared paper
Transfer your tally data into a bar chart. Use a ruler and colour the bars neatly.

4. Interpreting Graphs

Ask questions: Which category has the most? Which has the fewest? How many more…? What does the graph tell us about the class?

Critical thinking: Look at a graph where the scale starts at 5 instead of 0. Does it make differences look bigger? Discuss. (digital literacy and critical thinking).

Digital corner: Use a spreadsheet program (Excel/Sheets) to type in your tally data and insert a bar chart automatically. (digital literacy).

Exercise 4.1

  1. The tally for “Apple” shows 卌 ||. How many is that?
  2. Draw a pictograph for the following: Cricket – 6, Tennis – 4, Hockey – 8. Use 1 symbol = 2 people.
  3. From your pictograph, how many more people like hockey than tennis?
  4. Create a bar chart of the same data on squared paper.
  5. Write one question that your bar chart answers.

sessions.title: Probability – Chance Events
indicators: Describe the likelihood of everyday events using words: impossible, unlikely, likely, certain
Predict and test outcomes of simple experiments (e.g., tossing a coin, rolling a die)
Record and discuss results as a group, comparing predictions with actual outcomes (collaboration, communication)
Create a simple chance game and explain the rules (creativity)
Use digital probability simulators to run many trials quickly (digital literacy)
sessions.content:
Probability – What Are the Chances?

Probability is the study of how likely something is to happen. We use special words to describe the chance.

1. Chance Words

  • Impossible: will never happen. Example: A cow flying.
  • Unlikely: might happen but not very often. Example: Rain in the dry season.
  • Likely: will probably happen. Example: The sun will rise tomorrow.
  • Certain: will definitely happen. Example: You will grow older.

Activity 1 – Chance line
Draw a line from impossible to certain. Write events on cards (e.g., “Finding a 1000‑cedi note”, “A baby being born a boy”) and place them on the line. Discuss your choices. (collaboration, communication).

2. Experiments with Coins and Dice

Tossing a coin: It can land heads or tails. Both are equally likely. If you toss a coin 20 times, does heads come exactly 10 times? Try it!

Rolling a die: The outcomes are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Each number has an equal chance.

Activity 2 – Tally experiment
In pairs, toss a coin 30 times. Tally heads and tails. Compare your results with another pair. Did everyone get exactly 15 heads? Discuss why results vary. (collaboration, critical thinking).

3. Creating a Chance Game

Design a simple game that involves chance, like spinning a spinner or picking a coloured cube from a bag. Write the rules and explain how likely it is to win. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use an online coin‑flip simulator or die roller to run 100 tosses in seconds. Compare the digital results with your manual experiment. (digital literacy).

Exercise 4.2

  1. Is picking a red crayon from a box of only blue crayons impossible, unlikely, likely or certain?
  2. If you roll a die, what is the chance of rolling a 7? Explain.
  3. Toss a coin 10 times. Record your results. Was the number of heads close to 5?
  4. Place 3 red counters and 1 blue counter in a bag. Is it likely or unlikely to pull a red counter without looking?
  5. Describe an event that is certain to happen at school tomorrow.
